title: Detecting Suspicious Access to CRM Data in SaaS Environments
shortTitle: Detecting Suspicious Access to CRM Data in SaaS Environments
summary: This strategy covers Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship Management, meaning the theft of customer records, sales pipelines and contact data held in a SaaS CRM platform. It matters because CRM data is often the most valuable commercial asset a company holds and is frequently the reason attackers target business applications at all. The enabling telemetry lives in the SaaS audit trail: sign in events, API request logs, report and list view export records, bulk record read counts, permission and role changes, and connected application authorisations. The main way it fails in practice is that CRM platforms record that an export happened but not what was inside it, so analysts must lean on volume, timing, source address and the exporting account, and the data is only available if the tenant audit log or event monitoring product is enabled and retained.

beginner.definition: A CRM is software that stores customer details, deals and contact history. This detection watches for people or programs pulling large amounts of that data out of the platform. It looks at who exported records, from where, and how much they took.
beginner.whyItMatters: Customer lists are easy to sell and hard to replace. An attacker with a working CRM login can copy years of sales data in a few minutes. The platform may look healthy while this happens, because the account is valid. Catching the export while it runs gives you a chance to revoke access early.
howItWorks: The CRM platform writes an audit event for every sign in, every API call and every report or export action.
A SIEM, which is a central system that collects and searches log events, brings those events into one place.
The rule filters for export, report and bulk read actions rather than normal browsing.
It compares the number of records read with the normal amount for that user and that hour of the day.
It adds context, such as a new source address, a new device, or an unusual hour in the user's local time.
When the volume and the context both look wrong, the rule raises an alert for the identity team to review.
beginner.example: Imagine a public library where each visitor may read books on site. A visitor who photocopies the whole reference section in one night is not reading, they are copying. The library sign in sheet plus the photocopier counter is what proves it. In a CRM, the sign in event and the export record play exactly those two roles.
takeaways: CRM exports are normal, so the signal is volume, timing and source address, never the export itself.
Turn on the tenant audit log before an incident, because the events cannot be recovered later.
Tie every export alert to an account owner so someone can confirm whether the action was expected.

objectives: Describe how SaaS CRM audit trails record sign ins, API calls and record exports.
Distinguish legitimate sales reporting from bulk extraction using record counts and source context.
Correlate CRM sign in events with permission changes and connected application authorisations.
Explain why tenant audit logging must be enabled and retained for this detection to work at all.
Write tuning thresholds based on a per user baseline of normal export volume.
Identify which stakeholders to involve when a CRM data extraction alert fires.
dataSources: CRM platform audit log events for record export, report export and bulk list view actions with user, record count and source address
CRM sign in events including source address, device, client application and multi factor authentication result
CRM API gateway access logs recording endpoint, request volume and the calling integration or user token
CRM administrative audit events for role assignment, permission set change and connected app authorisation
Cloud identity provider sign in logs for the same account, used to check the sign in location against the CRM source address
logic: The pattern is a single account or API integration that reads far more customer records than its own history, especially when the reads come from a new address, a new client application or an hour outside the user's normal working window. To make this reliable you correlate the CRM export or bulk read event with the sign in event that produced the session, matching on user, session identifier and source address, and with any permission change or connected application authorisation in the preceding days. The benign case is a sales operations user running the same weekly report from the same office address with a stable record count, or a documented integration that pulls a fixed data set on a schedule. The malicious case tends to show a step change in volume, a report or export action by an account that has never exported before, or a source address that disagrees with the identity provider sign in location.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk CRM Record Export by Unusual Account
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection:
#     eventType:
#       - 'report.export'
#       - 'record.bulk_read'
#       - 'listview.export'
#   filter_known:
#     user|endswith: '@analytics.example.com'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known
#   threshold:
#     field: user
#     count: 5000
#     timeframe: 15m
# level: high
falsePositives: Sales operations staff running the standard weekly pipeline report, which legitimately exports several thousand rows
A scheduled marketing automation integration that pulls contact records on a fixed timer using a service account
Data migration or CRM consolidation projects where an administrator extracts whole objects on purpose
A sales manager downloading their team's quarter end data before a board meeting
Business intelligence connectors that refresh a warehouse table and therefore read large record sets every night
tuningNotes: Baseline export volume per account and per integration for at least one full business cycle, then alert on a multiple of that baseline rather than on an absolute row count. Maintain an allow list of known integration service accounts but keep alerting on interactive user exports above the threshold, and add the source address reputation and the sign in result as secondary conditions so a single offsite export at a conference does not page anyone. Scope the high severity rule to accounts with access to full customer objects and keep a lower severity version for the rest of the tenant. The coverage you lose by narrowing is slow extraction, where an attacker reads modest amounts every day to stay under the threshold, so also alert on a new first time exporter regardless of volume.
